speaker: Ross Taylor
quote_text: Hello and welcome to Stumped, your  intercontinental hit of news, features, and debate from the quirky world of cricket. I'm Alison  Mitchell and I'm in Northamptonshire in England. Well, the ECB - the England cricket board - now  need a new chief executive, alongside a whole host of other appointments they've made recently.  They have just got a white-ball coach secured from the international women's game, which is a very  interesting development. And I won't be here next week because I'm going to be off to commentate  on the French Open tennis, but I'm sure you will be put in excellent hands, nevertheless.  I'm Brett Sprigg here at the ABC in Sydney, where it's been a sombre week since learning of  the tragic and sudden passing of Andrey Symonds, which I know we'll talk about later on. On the  field, next summer is taking shape. It sounds like Cricket Australia wants to start its One  Day Internationals earlier in the day and finish before night-time to allocate more broadcast  time to the Big Bash. Whether such a move is able to revive that competition, time will tell.  But, I'm liking the fact that we won't have these 50-over games finishing so close to midnight  because nobody wants that, do they? Well, it does happen India all the time in the IPL.  Hi, I'm Charu Sharma, once again in Bangalore where it just can't stop raining. There's some  pre-monsoon madness and everything's flooded, including our basement by the way. We had some  midnight drama trying to get our cars away from there. Oh gosh. And of course, no golf, no tennis,  terrible stuff. But looks like we have to deal with another tragedy in the world of cricket.  Terrible about Andrew Symonds, and of course English cricket, I know Alison just can't seem  to get its act together. What's going on here? Let's hope they can get their act together in time  for that first Test match because that squad came out as well this week. Some interesting names. A  lot of people saying you know it's a bit of same, same going on, but we'll have time to talk about  that in the show as well of course reflects upon Andrew Symonds, because that's just too shocking  news and so soon off the back of Shane Warne as well and Rod Marsh even before that. Well, if  the legend that is Sachin Tendulkar describes you as "an inspiration for all the young kids  aspiring to be cricketers," you know you've made a pretty enormous impact. He has scored more  Test runs, more ODI, runs more ODI hundreds and overall hundreds than any other batter in  New Zealand history. He's recently retired after a long and distinguished international career. It  is the ex-captain and now former New Zealand bat, Ross Taylor. Ross, welcome to Stumped.  Hope you are well? That was a nice tweet from Sachin Tendulkar, wasn't it? And  you replied to him in Hindi, which was a classy touch. What did those words mean to you?  Thank you. Thanks for having me. Yeah, I must admit my Hindi translator Ish Sodhi  has been very good to me over the years and translating a few messages, as well  as replying to [Virender] Sehwag and co, and some other banter as well. But no, Sachin  has been an inspiration to a lot of players, and young kids growing up and I was no different.  He was one of my favourite players along with Mark Waugh growing up, so to have played against him a  few times, and to obviously have got that message is something I'll never forget.  I know you announced your international retirement back in December, but it's only last month when you  played your last game. We spoke to you on Stumped two years ago to mark your 100th Test match,  and 100 International appearances across all three formats as well, which does speak volumes  about the longevity of your career over those 16 years. And you said at the time, you know that the  R word was cropping up. I didn't say it, you did. But former players advised you that you are  a long-time retired. So, having played until the age of 38, what then made you decide  that, you know, now was the time to stop? I think everyone talks about the right time.   I think if you go on a little bit longer, I probably would have had to have committed to  play the next World Cup, and it just gives the next bunch of guys a few more opportunities  to play. Covid probably put a halt to that, it was pretty disjointed. Everyone in all parts  of the world were affected in different ways. When you're getting older and not being able to  play as often, it probably made me retire a little bit earlier than I probably would have liked,  but I'm really comfortable with my decision. I've enjoyed the time at home, but saying that I'm  still looking forward to playing a few tournaments around the world in the coming months. You came  over to England at quite a young age and had a very formative experience at Lord's. It seems quite fitting as we're talking to you only a couple in a week or so before New Zealand will  take on England at Lord's but tell us about that. I didn't really know much about Lord's to be fair.  I heard about the slope and coming from a population of 20,000 to the  population of London was definitely an eye opener. It was a good baptism of fire to really  pursue the career that I wanted to, to live and breathe cricket. To play at Lord's inspired me to  want to come back here and probably play County cricket and hopefully one day for New Zealand.  So, I was able to tick off a lot of those goals. I wasn't able to get on the honours board but a  few family members have gone through the the MCC tour over the years and apparently my name has  come up a few times for hitting a six over the the members side, so it couldn't have been all too bad!  You know, I was actually on one of those tours just yesterday Roscoe and your  name did come up, you're absolutely right! Obviously there's not many stories to tell but I  thought my family was just making it up! Your rise to the captaincy did happen pretty  quickly, of course. In 2010, you had your first taste of the national captaincy. Talk us through that, and I guess how you coped with that responsibility of that role initially? Yeah, I suppose it  was...I got it by default a little bit. I was vice captain. [Brendon] McCullum and  [Daniel] Vettori were on paternity leave. It was a strange one having to captain players  that are older than you, and significantly older than you. I'm half Samoan, and you always were  told to respect your elders. And it was really hard. I found it really hard to tell older  people who were in some cases a decade older me what to do. But no, I enjoyed the challenge.  I thought it brought the best out of my batting, but yeah, I suppose it was good. It was good  fun. Had some good results. But yeah, I guess, history will probably say something different.  Can I take you back to 2008? It was very special year for all of us, because that's when the IPL started  and give us some of your early memories because you mentioned the population of London. I presume  that even Bangalore and everything else about India was not easy to get used to Ross for you?  I was just ecstatic to go over. No one really knew what to expect. I didn't plan that first game. I  remember Martin Crowe said to me "Brendon McCullum was on the Red Bull's." He said "he's either going to  get a duck or 80!" I mean, Brendon ended up getting 158, which probably helped us out! But for me,  being the youngster sharing a dressing room with guys I'd watched on TV: [Rahul] Dravid, [Anil]  Kumble, [Jacques] Kallis, [Mark] Boucher, you know, guys that were legends of the game. I think  that helped my cricket and I think it helped New Zealand cricket. I think it broke down  the walls, the aura that these people had. We beat Mumbai & Sachin wasn't playing  but at the old Wankhede Stadium. I remember hitting Harbhajan [Singh] for a couple  of sixes. I didn't know which way the ball was going, so I just slogged it! A couple came out  of the middle and one landed on the roof! So, looking back on it, obviously once you retire,  you have fond memories, but at the same time I was pretty naive and pretty raw back  then and it probably wasn't a bad thing with everything else going around.  To have not had the full appreciation of what was going on. I'm sure you got your due the IPL  later but for the first year I do apologise I don't think we overpaid you  at all but I'm glad you came! Did you not clear the Chinnaswamy  Stadium as well? Because I mean, I remember you know all of us were marvelling at your bat speed.  It was it was fabulous! And tell us about some other memories... did the IPL help international  cricket as much as it perhaps did your career? Yeah, I think I get messages on my  Twitter and Instagram. I still have the sixth or seventh longest six. I don't know if  it counts because it was off a fellow Kiwi Jacob Oram. I remind him of that every now and  then. But yeah, as I said before, I think it definitely helped New Zealand cricket out. I think  the way all these players were playing, and other teams would. We used to put the Australia  and South Africa [players] on a pedestal, but once we saw them in action, yes they  were better than us but they weren't that far ahead of us. So, we knew what we needed  to do to get better. So, when we did play them it's sort of broke down their walls and you know  when Kallis and Boucher who you played with for years would end up sledging you but then laugh  afterwards sort of softened how things were, and I think for the benefit of cricket I think all that  other stuff actually helped out. I don't think New Zealand cricket is probably the only one, I think  a lot of other countries would have benefited from IPL and you know, right to the stage there's a lot  of players who are benefiting. New Zealand cricket are in fantastic shape, and I think a lot of  that's got down to having world class players but them getting the experience of rubbing shoulders  with these players that wouldn't have happened before IPL. And of course, I mean, we would seem  to think that that's a high point in your career, but will you consider it so winning the  World Test championships? The first one, always special? Yeah, I think so. I think to win  the inaugural one. People keep telling me why do you mention it? But after the heartbreak of 2019. Can I just say, I wasn't going to mention it! Yeah, that's why I'm bringing it up, because  it comes up anyway. You know, to come so close, it was a fantastic final at the home of cricket.  You're flying back home with all the emotions of the game and the what ifs. You also think  that's probably my last chance of playing in the World Cup and playing a World Cup final,  to two years later being in the same country, obviously different opposition but in a different format.  And then being there at the end with Kane [Williamson], and hitting the winning runs,  I couldn't have scripted it any better. I still get goosebumps thinking about it now. So, the Test series is about to start: England versus New Zealand. What did you  make of the appointment of Brendon McCullum to the England Test team role? And obviously your  relationship had its ups and downs throughout the year. I'm interested in did you sort of exchange  messages at the moment? Has he had any message from you or vice versa?  Yeah, I sent him a message once he got it to congratulate him. Two weeks ago, if you would have told me Brendon was going  to coach England, I would have said no chance. Then to coach a white-ball team, I probably would  have said, Oh, maybe. But the Test team? It's a complete surprise to a lot of New Zealanders. But  you know, it's no surprise that he interviewed well, and I think his combination with Stokes is  going to be an interesting one. There'll be, you know, very attacking. They're very similar minded  people, I think. And no, I'm just excited to see how they go. Obviously, because it's my  first series away, I was going to watch it with interest, but I think the added dimension  of Brendon being the coach. If there's any person that knows our team the best, it's going to  be him. I'm sure he's going to be passing on some inside information, so I'm sure  that in some ways it's going to be it's going to be his hardest test, but it could  also be his easiest in the way he can scout the team and know the nuances about how different  individuals play. And he's very good. He's very close with a lot of those players too, so I'm sure  that first morning of that Test, and when they do see each other, it's going to be a bit strange  for everyone. But I think he's going to do a fantastic role and I look forward to seeing  how him and Stokes and the rest of the team developed over the years. Congratulations on your international career, Ross and we really enjoyed chatting to you about it here on Stumped.  Thanks for having me. Next on Stumped, England's men's cricketers might not have played a match for a couple of months but goodness me it has been a busy time off the field. They've got  a new Test captain in Ben Stokes, new Test coach as we've been speaking about in Brendon McCullum,  and there's been even more this week. Tom Harrison resigned as chief executive, James Anderson and  Stuart Broad recalled to the Test squad for these first matches against New Zealand, and there's now  been the appointment of the new white-ball coach, which is Australia's highly successful women's  coach, Matthew Mott, on a four-year deal. Brett, does that come as a bit of a shock to Australians to lose Matthew Mott? Yes, because England's gain is certainly Australia's loss, Ali. Personally, I've been lucky enough to work with Motty on our ABC coverage of WBBL, where his unique  insights as national coach have been tremendous, and he's just a really lovely bloke. I'm happy  for him. Obviously, he's a popular coach, very team-first driven, very open to the evolution of  the game and certain game plans which are always, I guess, a cornerstone of white-ball and  particularly T20 cricket. So he would already have an idea of what sort of brand of cricket he  wants this England team to play. And indeed, who should be a part of its best XI. He presided over  three World Cup wins, three Ashes, that run on 26-straight One Day International wins, of course,  for the Aussie women as well. And let's not forget he had some previous coaching experience in the  UK. He was in charge of Glamorgan some years ago before the Australian gig. He also won a Sheffield  Shield here in New South Wales before that here in Australia. It's such a different scenario, Ali, I  guess to the Test side of things, where a bit of a rebuild happening. England is already reasonably  successful as the defending 50-over champions, currently ranked second, also ranked second in  T20s. Of course, interestingly, Matthew Mott's first big assignment in charge will be the T20  World Cup later this year in his home country. That's a great place to start. But yeah, a bit  of a shock, but that's certainly well deserved. Yeah, as regards the administration, Claire  Connor steps up as interim CEO for the ECB. So, that's quite a significant move as well. She  is the busiest woman in world cricket with her ICC role. I think her ECB women's role she  will step back a bit from that in order to take on the CEO role in the interim period, but I  would not be surprised at all if she put her hat in the ring for that role full time. She would be  absolutely qualified to step up. But there will be many, many other candidates as well. Or will  there because of course, English cricket is still in a little bit of a turbulent period, and  there is still long-standing division over The Hundred. There is still the aftermath and the  ongoing fallout from the Azeem Rafiq affair, and everything ECB is needing to do to  tackle discrimination in the game. So, there's a lot still churning away behind the  scenes, that's for sure. Brett, I did want to turn to the very sad news from Australia, more tragic  news with the loss of Andrew Symonds, who was just another dynamic cricketer in his day who  would become popular behind the mic, doing some commentary as well in recent years, too. He  was only 46 years old. Just tell us about the response down under.  Yeah, it's been as you can imagine, extremely deeply felt, given the other recent losses in particular Shane Warne from the  same era. Look, Andrew Symonds typified Australian iconicism. He could smack the ball around, he  bowled spin, he bowled pace. He was a world class fielder before we truly came to appreciate world  class fielders. He loved a beer, which is always endearing to the Australian public but perhaps  not so the Cricket Australia hierarchy at times. It's a shame that the so-called Monkeygate scandal  hastened his exit from international cricket, but the development no one ever talks about is  that he and Harbhajan Singh would go on to become teammates in the IPL and they got on quite well  in the end. So, there was a happy ending there, even if the legacy of that saga serves to remind  us that Cricket Australia was prepared to put its business interests ahead of the welfare one of its  players. It's so disappointing that his career was tainted by that through no fault of his, but  Aussie cricket fans remember Andrew Symonds so fondly. Certainly, Queenslanders do. I was up  in Queensland when the news broke, and there were 40,000 fans at a Rugby League match I was at  that observed a pure moment silence. The respect was always there for him, and I just feel for his  family obviously, and his children are only still quite young, primary school age. But again, it's a  loss at the cricket community will feel together. Yeah, well, I've heard Harbhajan Singh  particularly recalled some fond memories later on when they became colleagues and I think all of  India particularly appreciated his enormous skill, his genius really with the bat and he was  pretty handy bowler as well and Brett, you mentioned his fielding, so an all-round  cricketer, you know. One of the best in the world. The fact that he went so soon and  after some other icons too, it's truly tragic. Well, that is it for Stumped this week on All  India Radio. Don't forget you can follow us on Twitter, we're @BBCWSSport and use #BBCStumped.  Check us out on YouTube as well, go to the BBC World Service's YouTube channel. My thanks to  Charu Sharma and to Brett Sprigg, and, of course, to our special guest, Ross Taylor, and you for  listening. We'll see you next week. Bye bye.
title: Ross Taylor: Retirement, New Zealand and McCullum's England - Stumped, BBC World Service
